title: Network Topologies: Hybrid, Multicloud, and VPC Design
bodyMarkdown:
## Why network topology comes first

Every later provisioning decision (load balancers, storage access, GKE Pod ranges, ML endpoints) inherits the network you build first. Addressing mistakes are the hardest thing to fix afterwards, because a subnet range or a peering relationship that overlaps another one blocks connectivity permanently until you rebuild it. For the exam, treat this module as a set of matching problems: a requirement (central governance, private SaaS access, 99.99% hybrid link, multicloud analytics) maps to exactly one primitive.

## VPC fundamentals

A [VPC network](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc) is a **global** resource, and its **subnets are regional**. One VPC can therefore span every region, and VMs in `us-central1` and `europe-west1` reach each other over private IPs on Google's backbone with no VPN between them. Key facts the exam relies on:

- **Auto mode** creates one subnet per region automatically from the `10.128.0.0/9` block, and adds subnets as new regions launch. The `default` network is auto mode. Auto mode cannot hold IPv6 ranges.
- **Custom mode** creates nothing automatically; you choose regions and ranges. Converting auto to custom is a one-way change, and a custom network can never be converted back.
- Every primary or secondary IPv4 range must be a unique, valid CIDR block, and **four IP addresses in each primary subnet range are unusable** (reserved by Google).
- The organization policy `compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation` stops new projects from getting the `default` network. Enterprise landing zones normally enable it and use custom mode only.
- Firewalling has two implied rules: ingress to a VM is **denied** and egress is **allowed** unless you add rules.

Secondary ranges matter for GKE: VPC-native clusters take Pod and Service addresses from secondary ranges on the subnet, so size them up front (module 4 covers the details).

**Planning rule:** allocate one non-overlapping RFC 1918 plan for the whole organization, including on-premises and other clouds, before creating any VPC. Overlap is what breaks Peering, VPN and Interconnect routing later.

## Choosing how networks and services connect

| Requirement | Pattern | Key property |
|---|---|---|
| Central network team owns subnets and firewalls; app teams run in their own projects | [Shared VPC](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/shared-vpc) | One host project, many service projects, same organization |
| Join two independently administered VPCs with non-overlapping ranges | [VPC Network Peering](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/vpc-peering) | Non-transitive; no overlapping subnets; firewalls not shared |
| Consume or publish one specific service privately, with possibly overlapping IP space | [Private Service Connect](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/private-service-connect) | One-way consumer to producer; NAT between sides; no peering |
| Hub-and-spoke across many VPCs and on-premises sites | [Network Connectivity Center](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/network-connectivity-center/concepts/overview) | VPC spokes and hybrid spokes through one hub |

### Shared VPC

A host project contains one or more Shared VPC networks that a Shared VPC Admin has enabled for sharing; a service project is any project attached to a host project. The constraints worth memorizing:

- All participating projects must be in the **same organization**.
- A service project attaches to **only one** host project, and a project cannot be both host and service. An organization can still run several host projects (for example one per environment).
- You can share all subnets (including future ones) or select specific subnets.
- Access is granted with `compute.networkUser` (the Service Project Admin role). Granted at project level it covers every shared subnet; granted at subnet level it restricts a team to those subnets.
- The Shared VPC Admin role is built from `compute.xpnAdmin` plus `resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin`.

This is the default answer when a scenario says "central control of subnets and firewall policy, teams deploy in their own projects".

### VPC Network Peering

Peering joins two VPCs administratively separate from each other. Three limits decide most questions:

- It is **not transitive**: if `net-a` peers with `net-b` and with `net-c`, `net-b` and `net-c` still cannot talk.
- No subnet range in one network may exactly match, contain, or sit inside a range in the peered network. Google Cloud enforces this at peering time and when you create new subnets.
- Firewall rules and policies are **not exchanged**. Subnet routes are always exchanged; static and dynamic custom routes only if you export and import them (`--export-custom-routes` and `--import-custom-routes`).

A full mesh of peerings between many business units is the classic wrong answer: it explodes in count and still cannot be transitive.

### Private Service Connect

Private Service Connect (PSC) is service-oriented rather than network-oriented. The producer publishes a service (behind a load balancer) with a **service attachment** that defines an accept list, NAT subnets and optional DNS. The consumer creates an **endpoint**, which is a forwarding rule with an internal IP in the consumer VPC that references the service attachment. Other PSC flavors: **backends** (network endpoint groups so a load balancer can front a managed service) and **interfaces** (let a producer initiate connections into the consumer network, the one case that reverses direction).

Because traffic is NATed between the two sides, there is **no IP coordination and no peering required**, and access is authorized per service, not per network. PSC also reaches Google APIs privately (global, regional and multi-regional endpoints), which is the usual answer for "reach Google APIs without internet egress".

### Network Connectivity Center

Network Connectivity Center (NCC) is a hub-and-spoke control plane. Spoke types include **VPC spokes** (which can reference networks across projects and organizations), **hybrid spokes** (HA VPN tunnels, Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachments, router appliance VMs), producer VPC spokes and gateway spokes. Hybrid spokes can re-advertise imported routes, which provides site-to-site transit using Google's network as a WAN. Constraints: Classic VPN is not supported, BGP communities are not supported, and in a site-to-site setup all hybrid spokes must be in the same VPC network.

## Hybrid connectivity

| Option | Transport | Capacity | Pick when |
|---|---|---|---|
| [HA VPN](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/vpn/concepts/overview) | IPsec over the internet | Each tunnel up to 250,000 packets per second, roughly 1 to 3 Gbps | Fast start, moderate throughput, or encrypted backup path |
| [Dedicated Interconnect](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/dedicated-overview) | Private fiber you cross-connect in a colocation facility | 10, 100 or 400 Gbps circuits, up to 8 per connection | High, steady bandwidth; you can reach a Google colocation facility |
| [Partner Interconnect](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/partner-overview) | Through a service provider | 10 or 100 Gbps circuits, up to 8 | You cannot reach a Dedicated site, or you do not need a full 10 Gbps |
| [Cross-Cloud Interconnect](https://cloud.google.com/network-connectivity/docs/interconnect/concepts/cci-overview) | Google-provisioned link to another cloud | 10 or 100 Gbps; 400 Gbps for AWS and OCI | Private, high-bandwidth path to AWS, Azure, OCI or Alibaba Cloud |

**HA VPN** uses a gateway with two interfaces, requires dynamic routing (BGP) through Cloud Router, and offers a 99.99% SLA for most topologies when configured with the documented redundant layout (Classic VPN is 99.9% and static). It supports IKEv1 and IKEv2 with pre-shared keys. **HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect** gives IPsec encryption on the private path with no internet transit. Interconnect itself is not encrypted by default; **MACsec for Cloud Interconnect** adds link-level encryption.

**Dedicated Interconnect** needs single-mode fiber, LACP, EBGP multi-hop and 802.1Q VLANs at your edge, and the link type chosen at creation cannot be changed later. Jumbo frames (MTU 8896) work only on unencrypted attachments.

### Redundancy topologies decide the SLA

The published SLA is a property of the topology, not of the product tier:

- **99.99% (critical production):** at least **four** connections, two in one metro and two in another, with the pair in each metro in different edge availability domains. For the multi-region layout you also need four VLAN attachments across two regions, at least two Cloud Routers (one per region) and **global dynamic routing mode**.
- **99.9% (non-critical):** at least two connections in the same metro but different edge availability domains.
- **Partner Interconnect** follows the same shape: four VLAN attachments across two metros in separate edge availability domains, two Cloud Routers, global routing for 99.99%.
- A single-region 99.99% layout also exists (four connections across two zone-paired facilities in one metro, `PRODUCTION_CRITICAL`), but the multi-metro layout is what most questions describe.

Exam wording usually says "two metropolitan areas, redundant connections in separate edge availability domains". The principle is no single point of failure at the cable, the edge domain, the metro, or the Cloud Router. A single connection, or two connections in one edge domain, never earns 99.99%.

## Multicloud patterns

For analytics over data that lives in another cloud, prefer querying it in place. [BigQuery Omni](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/omni-introduction) runs the BigQuery engine in AWS or Azure regions against Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage data through BigLake tables, serverless, with no raw-data copy to Google Cloud. It requires the Enterprise edition, uses AWS IAM roles or Azure AD principals for access, and has limits (no BigQuery ML, DML or JavaScript UDFs; cross-cloud transfers via joins or SELECT are capped at 60 GB each). When you must move data, use materialized views for continuous filtered replication or `LOAD` for bulk migration.

For network reach between clouds, use Cross-Cloud Interconnect (private, Google-provisioned) and NCC to avoid a full mesh of point-to-point links. Customers buy ports from both Google Cloud and the other provider.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Overlapping ranges "fixed later".** Peering and most hybrid topologies refuse or misroute overlapping CIDRs. Use PSC if overlap is unavoidable between a consumer and a specific producer.
- **Peering as a transit hub.** Peering is non-transitive; use Shared VPC for governance, NCC for hub-and-spoke.
- **One flat VPC with Owner for everyone.** Defeats centralized firewall and subnet control; Shared VPC with subnet-level `compute.networkUser` is the intended answer.
- **Treating one Interconnect as highly available.** One connection, or two connections in the same edge availability domain, carries no 99.99% SLA.
- **Forgetting Cloud Router modes.** Multi-region 99.99% layouts need global dynamic routing; regional mode does not meet the requirement.
- **Using auto mode in production.** Predefined ranges from `10.128.0.0/9` collide with on-premises and other VPCs. Create custom-mode networks.
- **Copying data nightly to query it.** For occasional cross-cloud analytics, BigQuery Omni avoids the copy, the storage duplication and the ETL cluster.
- **Assuming Interconnect is encrypted.** It is private, not encrypted, unless you add MACsec or HA VPN over Interconnect.

## Exam tips

- **Shared VPC is the governance answer.** "Network team owns subnets and firewalls, app teams deploy in their own projects" means host and service projects, same organization, `compute.networkUser` per subnet.
- **Peering is non-transitive and needs non-overlapping ranges.** If a scenario has many VPCs needing any-to-any reachability or overlapping CIDRs, Peering is the distractor.
- **PSC means service-level, one-way, no peering.** Endpoint equals a forwarding rule with an internal IP pointing at a service attachment; it also reaches Google APIs privately.
- **99.99% Interconnect equals redundancy in two metros.** Four connections or attachments, separate edge availability domains, two Cloud Routers and global routing. One connection never qualifies.
- **Pick the link by reachability and size.** Colocation reachable and steady load means Dedicated; no colocation or under 10 Gbps means Partner; quick or backup means HA VPN (about 1 to 3 Gbps per tunnel).
- **Another cloud's private path is Cross-Cloud Interconnect.** AWS, Azure, OCI and Alibaba Cloud are supported; multi-site transit uses NCC.
- **Analytics across clouds is BigQuery Omni.** Query in place, serverless, Enterprise edition; do not pick nightly exports or self-managed Spark.
- **Encryption on a private link is an add-on.** MACsec for link-level, HA VPN over Interconnect for IPsec.
